About the Course





This course is an advanced study that follows Data Structures and Algorithms. It is designed to equip students with a deep understanding of major algorithmic design paradigms and the techniques required for their rigorous analysis. The curriculum covers the formal analysis of algorithm correctness, time complexity, and space complexity, as well as computational complexity theory including NP‑completeness.

Lemma 1 (Cycle Property). Let \(C\) be any cycle, and let \(f\) be the maximum cost edge belonging to \(C\). Then the MST \(T^*\) does not contain \(f\).


Proof. Proof. Suppose \(f \in T^*\). Deleting \(f\) disconnects \(T^*\). Let \(S\) be one side of the cut. Some other edge \(e \in C\) has exactly one endpoint in \(S\), and \(T = T^* \cup \{e\} - \{f\}\) is a spanning tree of lower cost — a contradiction. ◻

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Worst-case analysis

Let \(T(n)\) be the worst-case time for the procedure RANDOMIZED-QUICKSORT on an input of size \(n\).

We have the recurrence: \[T(n) = \mbox{max}_{0\leq q\leq n-1}(T(q) + T(n-q-1)) + \Theta(n).\]

We guess that \(T(n)\leq cn^2\).
We use substitution method to prove the worst-case complexity.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Worst-case analysis continued...
Substituting the guess into recurrence, we obtain \[\begin{aligned}
    T(n) &\leq \mbox{max}_{0\leq q\leq n-1}(cq^2+c(n-q-1)^2) + \Theta(n)\\
        &=c\mbox{max}_{0\leq q\leq n-1}(q^2+(n-q-1)^2) + \Theta(n)
\end{aligned}\] Let, \[\begin{aligned}
    f(q) &= q^2+(n-q-1)^2\\
    f'(q) &= 2q-2(n-q-1) = 4q-2n+2\\
    f''(q) &= 4.
\end{aligned}\]

\(f'(q) = 0\) when \(q = \frac{n-1}{2}\).
\(f'(q)\) is continuous.
\(f''(q)\) is positive meaning that \(f(q)\) has a local minima at \(q = \frac{n-1}{2}\).
This implies \(f(q)\) is maximum at \(q=0\) and \(q=(n-1)\).
\(f(0) = f(n-1) = (n-1)^2\).

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Worst-case analysis continued...
Coming back to recurrence: \[\begin{aligned}
    T(n) &\leq c(n-1)^2 + \Theta(n) \\
        &= cn^2 - c(2n-1) + \Theta(n) \\
        &\leq cn^2.
\end{aligned}\] Therefore, \(T(n) = O(n^2)\).
Exercise: Show that \(T(n)=\Omega(n^2)\).

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Points to remember

Warning-1: It is easier to prove a weaker bound than the one you are supposed to prove. For instance, if the runtime is \(O(n)\), you might still be able to substitute \(cn^2\) into the recurrence and prove that the bound is \(O(n^2)\). Although it is technically correct, don’t let it mislead you into thinking it’s the best bound!
Warning-2: You must prove the exact form of the induction hypothesis. For example, in the recurrence \(T(n) = 2T(\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor)+n\), we could falsely prove \(T(n) = O(n)\) by guessing \(T(n)\leq cn\) and then arguing \(T(n)\leq 2(c\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor)+n\leq cn+n = O(n)\). Here we need to prove \(T(n)\leq cn\), not \(T(n)\leq (c+1)n\).

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Recursion Tree for solving recurrences:

A recursion tree is a tree where each node represents the cost of certain recursive subproblem. Then we sum up the numbers in each node to get the cost.
We will use a recursion tree for to generate possible guesses for the runtime, and then use the substitution method to prove them.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Recursion Tree
Consider the following recurrence:


\(T(n)=3T(\lfloor\frac{n}{4}\rfloor)+\Theta(n^2)\)

Let us drop the floors and write the recurrence:

\(T(n)=3T(\frac{n}{4})+cn^2\)

image

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Recursion Tree

Suppose the number of levels in this tree is \(l\).
\(\frac{n}{4^l} = 1\). This implies \(l = \log_4{n}\).
Number of leaf nodes: \(3^{\log_4{n}} = n^{\log_4{3}}\).

\[\begin{aligned}
    T(n)    &= cn^2+\frac{3}{16}cn^2+(\frac{3}{16})^2cn^2+\cdots+(\frac{3}{16})^{\log_4{n}-1}cn^2 + \Theta(n^{\log_4{3}}) \\
        &= \displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{\log_4{n}-1}(\frac{3}{16})^icn^2 + \Theta(n^{\log_4{3}}) \\
    &\leq \displaystyle\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}(\frac{3}{16})^icn^2 + \Theta(n^{\log_4{3}}) \\
    &= (1-3/16)^{-1}cn^2 + \Theta(n^{\log_4{3}})
\end{aligned}\]
Since the functions in \(\Theta(n^{\log_4{3}})\) are also in \(O(n^2)\), This whole expression is \(O(n^2)\). Therefore we can guess that \(T(n) = O(n^2)\).

We want to show that \(T(n)\leq dn^2\) for some constant \(d > 0\). $$

            &\leq 3d\lfloor\frac{n}{4}\rfloor^2 + cn^2 \\
            &\leq 3d(\frac{n}{4})^2 + cn^2 \\
            &= \frac{3}{16}dn^2 + cn^2 \\
            &\leq dn^2 (\text{ when } c\leq \frac{13}{16}d)

Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP)
Problem: Given a set of cities along with the cost of travel between them, find the cheapest route visiting all cities and returning to your starting point.
Formal Definition: Given a complete undirected graph \(G = (V, E)\) with nonnegative integer cost \(c(u,v)\) for each edge \((u,v) \in E\), find a Hamiltonian cycle of \(G\) with minimum cost.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
TSP: Special Instances
Metric TSP: Costs satisfy the triangle inequality: \[c(u,w) \le c(u,v) + c(v,w) \quad \text{for all } u,v,w \in V\]
Euclidean TSP: Cities are points in Euclidean space, costs equal to their Euclidean distance.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Hardness of Approximation
Theorem: TSP cannot be approximated within any polynomial factor (unless P = NP).
Proof Idea: Reduction from the Hamiltonian-cycle problem.
Let \(G = (V, E)\) be an instance of Hamiltonian-cycle. Construct a complete graph \(G' = (V, E')\) with costs: - If \((u,v) \in E\), then \(c(u,v) = 1\) - If \((u,v) \notin E\), then \(c(u,v) = \text{(large)}\)

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Hardness of Approximation: Proof
If \(G\) has a Hamiltonian cycle \(H\), then \((G', c)\) contains a tour of cost \(|V|\).
If \(G\) does not have a Hamiltonian cycle, then any tour \(T\) must use some edge not in \(E\), incurring a large cost.
This gap makes it impossible to approximate unless P = NP.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Metric TSP: Approximation Algorithm
Idea: First compute an MST, then create a tour based on the tree.
APPROX-TSP-TOUR: 1. Compute a minimum spanning tree \(T_{\min}\) of \(G\). 2. Let \(W\) be a full walk of \(T_{\min}\) (traverses each edge twice). 3. Remove duplicate vertices from \(W\) to obtain a Hamiltonian cycle \(H\).
Runtime is dominated by MST-PRIM: \(\Theta(V^2)\).

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
2-Approximation Proof
Theorem: APPROX-TSP-TOUR is a polynomial-time 2-approximation algorithm for Metric TSP.
Consider the optimal tour \(H^*\) and remove an arbitrary edge. This yields a spanning tree \(T\) with: \[c(T) \le c(H^*)\]
(All edge costs are non-negative.)

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
2-Approximation Proof (contd.)
Let \(W\) be the full walk of the minimum spanning tree \(T_{\min}\).

The full walk traverses each edge exactly twice, so \(c(W) = 2c(T_{\min})\).
Since \(T_{\min}\) is an MST: \(c(T_{\min}) \le c(T) \le c(H^*)\).
Therefore: \(c(W) = 2c(T_{\min}) \le 2c(H^*)\).

Deleting duplicate vertices from \(W\) yields a tour \(H\) with cost no larger than \(W\) (by triangle inequality). - So \(c(H) \le c(W) \le 2c(H^*)\).

General TSP cannot be approximated (unless P = NP)
Metric TSP has a simple 2-approximation using MST
Algorithm: MST → full walk → shortcut duplicates
Proof uses triangle inequality and MST optimality
Runtime: \(O(V^2)\) (dominated by MST computation)

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms

Introduction
What to do when we want to solve an NP-Complete (optimization) problem?

Exact Algorithm: Guarantees optimal solution. Runtime not polynomial, but fast enough for many instances.
Heuristic: Algorithms without guarantees on solution quality.
Approximation Algorithms: Algorithms that compute a solution with a quality guarantee within a certain factor from OPT.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Terminologies: Minimization
Consider a minimization problem:

OPT(\(I\)): value of the optimal solution for instance \(I\)
ALG(\(I\)): value computed by algorithm ALG for instance \(I\)

ALG is a \(\rho\)-approximation algorithm if: \[\text{ALG}(I) \le \rho \cdot \text{OPT}(I) \quad \text{for all inputs } I\]
\(\rho\) is called the approximation factor.
Example: Vertex Cover — if ALG computes a cover with at most twice the minimum, then ALG is a 2-approximation.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Terminologies: Maximization
Consider a maximization problem:
ALG is a \(\rho\)-approximation algorithm if: \[\text{ALG}(I) \ge \frac{1}{\rho} \cdot \text{OPT}(I) \quad \text{for all inputs } I\]
Example: CLIQUE — if ALG computes a clique with at least half the maximum size, then ALG is a 2-approximation.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Proving Approximation Guarantees
For a \(\rho\)-approximation algorithm ALG we must:

Describe the algorithm
Analyze running time
Prove that \(\text{ALG}(I) \le \rho \cdot \text{OPT}(I)\) for all inputs \(I\)

Challenge: How to prove this bound without knowing OPT?
Solution: Find a lower bound on OPT(\(I\)).
Example: If OPT \(\ge 100\) and ALG \(\le 200\), then ALG \(\le 2\cdot\text{OPT}\).

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms

Approximation Scheme
Takes two inputs: - An instance of the problem - A value \(\epsilon > 0\)
Goal: Design a \((1+\epsilon)\)-approximation algorithm.

PTAS (Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme): Runs in time polynomial in \(n\) (for fixed \(\epsilon\)). Runtime may increase rapidly as \(\epsilon\) decreases, e.g., \(O(n^{2/\epsilon})\).
FPTAS (Fully Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme): Runs in time polynomial in both \(1/\epsilon\) and \(n\), e.g., \(O((1/\epsilon)^2 n^3)\).

Optimization problem: Find a vertex cover with minimum number of vertices.
Vertex Cover is NP-hard.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms

Repeatedly pick a vertex of highest degree and remove all incident edges.
Problem: Might select wrong vertices, leading to bad approximation.
Approximation ratio can be as bad as \(|V| - 1\).

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms

APPROX-VERTEX-COVER: - While there are edges in \(G\): - Pick any edge \((u,v)\) from \(G\). - Add both \(u\) and \(v\) to the cover. - Remove all edges incident to \(u\) or \(v\) from \(G\).
Theorem: APPROX-VERTEX-COVER is a polynomial-time 2-approximation algorithm.

Set Covering Problem
Given a finite set \(X\) and a family \(F\) of subsets of \(X\) such that every element of \(X\) belongs to at least one subset in \(F\), find a subset of \(F\) that covers all elements of \(X\).
Optimization: Find \(S \subseteq F\) of minimum size that covers \(X\).
Set Cover is NP-hard — a generalization of Vertex Cover.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms

Greedy choice: At each stage, pick the set that covers the most uncovered elements.
Theorem: The greedy heuristic achieves an approximation factor of \(\ln m\), where \(m\) is the total number of elements in the original set.

Halting Problem
Given a computer program, does it ever halt?

Uncomputable (not in R): There is no algorithm for solving this.
Decision problem: The answer is either YES or NO.

Proved by Alan Turing (and Alonzo Church) in 1936.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Halting Problem is Undecidable
Proof by contradiction: Assume algorithm \(H(P,I)\) solves the halting problem.
Construct \(X(P)\) that takes a program \(P\) as input:

If \(H(X,X)\) returns YES, then \(X\) does not halt on \(X\). (Contradiction)
If \(H(X,X)\) returns NO, then \(X\) halts on \(X\). (Contradiction)

Therefore, \(H\) cannot exist.

To show \(X\) is NP-complete:

Step 1: Show \(X\) is in NP — design a polytime verifier.
Step 2: Pick a known NP-complete problem \(Y\).
Step 3: Construct an algorithm to solve \(Y\) given an algorithm to solve \(X\).
Step 4: Prove correctness of your algorithm.

Input: Given a graph \(G\) and an integer \(k\).

\(S\) is an independent set by verifying no two vertices in \(S\) are adjacent.
The size of \(S\) is at least \(k\).

Given a 3-CNF formula \(\phi\) with \(k\) clauses, build a graph \(G\) such that \(\phi\) is satisfiable iff \(G\) has an independent set of size \(k\).

There will be \(3k\) vertices (one triple per clause).
Each clause contributes 3 edges connecting its literals.
For each pair of nodes representing opposite literals, there is an edge.

text:
Recurrence for Divide and Conquer
A recurrence for the running time of a divide-and-conquer algorithm falls out from the three steps of the basic paradigm. Suppose \(\mathbf{T(n)}\) be the running time on a problem of size \(n\).

Suppose that our division of the problem yields \(\mathbf{a}\) subproblems, each of which is \(\mathbf{1/b}\) the size of the original.

It takes time \(\mathbf{T(n/b)}\) to solve one subproblem of size \(\mathbf{n/b}\), and so it takes time \(\mathbf{aT(n/b)}\) to solve \(\mathbf{a}\) of them.

If we take \(\mathbf{D(n)}\) time to divide the problem into subproblems, and \(\mathbf{C(n)}\) time to combine the solutions to the subproblems into the solution to the original problem, we get the recurrence: \[T(n) = \begin{cases}
            \Theta(1) & \mbox{ if } n\leq c \\
            aT(n/b) + D(n) + C(n) & \mbox{ otherwise }
    \end{cases}\]

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Analysis of merge sort
We reason as follows to set up the recurrence for \(T(n)\):

Divide: The divide step just computes the middle of the subarray, which takes constant time. Thus, \(D(n)=\Theta(1)\).
Conquer: We recursively solve two subproblems, each of size \(n/2\), which contributes \(2T(n/2)\) to the running time.
Combine: MERGE procedure on an \(n\)-element subarray takes time \(\Theta(n)\), and so \(C(n)=\Theta(n)\).

Thus, we get the following recurrence relation of merge sort: \[T(n) = \begin{cases}
        \Theta(1) & \mbox{ if } n=1, \\
        2T(n/2) + \Theta(n) & \mbox{ if } n>1,
    \end{cases}\]

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Analysis of merge sort
We can rewrite the recurrence as follows: \[T(n) = \begin{cases}
        c & \mbox{ if } n=1, \\
        2T(n/2) + cn & \mbox{ if } n>1,
    \end{cases}\] where the constant \(c\) represents the time required to solve problems of size \(1\) as well as the time per array element of the divide and combine step.
We can solve this recurrence using a recursion tree.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms

Analysis of merge sort

The number of levels of the recursion tree is \(\log_2{n}+1\) where \(n\) is the number of leaves.


We can prove this by using induction on the number of leaf nodes.
Base Case: When \(n=1\), the number of levels is \(\log_2{1}+1 = 1\) which is true.
Inductive Hypothesis: Assume that the number of levels of a recursion tree with \(2^n\) leaves is \(\log_2(2^n)+1 = n+1\).
Inductive Step: Because we are assuming that the input size is a power of \(2\), the next input size to consider is \(2^{n+1}\). A tree with \(l=2^{n+1}\) leaves has one more level than a tree with \(2^n\) leaves, and so the total number of levels is \((n+1)+1 = \log_2{2^{n+1}}+1\).

Following the above result, \(T(n) = cn\log_2{n}+cn\). Ignoring the low order term and the constant \(c\) gives us \(T(n) = \Theta(n\log{n})\).

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Network Flow Problem
We are given a directed graph \(G = (V, E)\), a start node \(s\), and a sink node \(t\). Each edge \(e\) in \(G\) has an associated non-negative capacity \(c(e)\), where for all non-edges it is implicitly assumed that the capacity is \(0\). For example, consider the following graph:




image



Goal: Push as much flow as possible from \(s\) to \(t\) n the graph. The rules are that no edge can have flow exceeding its capacity, and for any vertex except for \(s\) and \(t\), the flow in to the vertex must equal the flow out from the vertex. Formally,

Capacity constraint: On any edge we have flow \(f(e)\leq c(e)\).
Flow conservation: For any vertex \(v\notin\{s, t\}\), flow in equal flow out: \(\sum_{u}f(u, v) = \sum_{u}f(v, u)\).

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms

Network Flow Problem

When \((u,v)\notin E\), there can be no flow from \(u\) to \(v\), and \(f(u,v)=0\).
We call a non negative quantity \(f(u, v)\) the flow from vertex \(u\) to vertex \(v\).
The value \(|f|\) of a flow \(f\) is defined as \(|f| = \sum_{v}f(s, v) - \sum_{v}f(v, s)\).
Typically, a flow network will not have any edge into the source, and therefore, \(\sum_{v}f(v, s)\), will be \(0\).
\(\sum_{v}f(v, s)\) will be significant in case of residual network (we will discuss later).

Maximum-flow Problem: Given a flow network \(G\), with source \(s\) and sink \(t\), find a flow of maximum value.

Accounting method (banker’s method)
Assign different charges to each operation.

\(D_i:\) data structure after \(i^{th}\) operation.
\(c_i:\) actual cost of \(i^{th}\) operation.
\(\hat{c_i}:\) amortized cost of \(i^{th}\) operation = amount we charge operation \(i\).
When \(\hat{c_i} > c_i\), we store credits in data structure \(D_i\) to pay for future operations.
When \(\hat{c_i} < c_i\), we consume credits in data structure \(D_i\).
Initial data structure \(D_0\) starts with \(0\) credits.

Credit invariant: The total number of credits in the data structure at any point \(\geq 0\).

\(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^t\hat{c_i} - \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^t c_i\geq 0\).


Otherwise, total amortized cost after \(t\) operations is less than the total actual cost, so if the subsequent operation do not give enough credit to makeup for it, the condition of amortized cost being upper bound of the actual cost will get violated.

Credits: One credit pays for a bit flip.
Accounting:

Flip bit \(j\) from \(0\) to \(1\): charge \(2\) credits (use one and save one in bit \(j\)).
Flip bit \(j\) from \(1\) to \(0\): pay for it with the one credit saved in bit \(j\).

Theorem. Starting from zero counter, a sequence of \(n\) INCREMENT operations flips \(O(n)\) bits.
Proof. Each increment operation flips at most one \(0\) bit to a \(1\) bit. So, the amortized cost per INCREMENT \(\leq 2\).
Following credit invariant, Total actual cost of \(n\) operations \(\leq\) sum of amortized costs \(\leq 2n\).

Potential function: \(\Phi(D_i)\) maps each data structure \(D_i\) to a real number such that

\(\Phi(D_0) = 0\).
\(\Phi(D_i)\geq 0\) for each data structure \(D_i\).

Actual and amortized costs:

\(c_i =\) actual cost of \(i^{th}\) operation.
\(\hat{c_i} = c_i + \Phi(D_i) - \Phi(D_{i-1}) =\) amortized cost of \(i^{th}\) operation (actual cost + potential change).
Total amortized cost \[\begin{aligned}
    \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n\hat{c_i}  &= \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n [c_i + \Phi(D_i) - \Phi(D_{i-1})] \\
                & = \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n c_i + \Phi(D_n) - \Phi(D_0)
\end{aligned}\]

We need \(\Phi(D_n)\geq\Phi(D_0)\).
This is true for any \(n\), so, we need \(\Phi(D_i)\geq\Phi(D_0)\) for any \(i\).

Assign potential of the \(k\)-bit counter after \(i\)-th increment \(\Phi(D_i)=b_i\), the number of \(1\)’s in the counter.
So \(\Phi(D_i)\geq 0\) for any \(i\).
Compute the amortized cost of an increment

Suppose the \(i^{th}\) operation resets \(t_i\) bits.
Actual cost \(c_i\) is at most \(t_i+1\).
if \(b_i > 0\) then \(b_{i} \leq b_{i-1} - t_i+1\).


Thus amortized cost \(\hat{c_i} = c_i + \Phi(D_i) - \Phi(D_{i-1}) \leq c_i + 1 - t_i = 2\). Therefore, the total amortized cost of \(n\) INCREMENT is \(O(n)\) and average cost per increment is \(O(1)\).

Introduction - Asymptotic analysis

The order of growth of the running time of an algorithm gives a simple characterization of the algorithm’s efficiency.
Asymptotic efficiency: We are concerned with how the running time of an algorithm increases with the size of the input in the limit, as the size of the input inreases without bound.
An algorithm is asymptotically more efficient will be the best choice for all but very small inputs.
Asymptotic running time of an algorithm are defined in terms of functions whose domains are the set of natural numbers \(N=\{0, 1, 2, \ldots\}\). Such notations are convenient for describing the worst-case running-time funcion \(T(n)\), which is usually defined only on integer input sizes.

Prim’s Algorithm
In this algorithm, we start with a node and grow an MST out of it.
We start with an arbitrary node \(u\) and include it in \(T\). We then find the lowest-weight edge incident on \(u\) and add this to \(T\). We then repeat, always adding the minimum-weight edge that has exactly one endpoint in \(T\) to \(T\). Formal description of the algorithm is as follows:

Pick some arbitrary start node \(u\). Initialize \(T=\{u\}\).
Repeatedly pick the lowest-weight edge incident to \(T\) that has exactly one vertex is in \(T\) until \(T\) spans all nodes.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Correctness of Prim’s Algorithm

Prim’s algorithm correctly computes an MST


Proof. Proof. We’ll prove this by induction. The induction hypothesis will be that after each iteration, the tree \(T\) is a subgraph of some minimum spanning tree \(M\). This is trivially true at the start, since initially \(T\) is just a single node and no edges. Now suppose that at some point in the algorithm we have \(T\) which is a subgraph of \(M\), and Prim’s algorithm tells us to add the edge \(e\). So we need to prove that \(T\cup\{e\}\) is also a subtree of some MST. If \(e\in M\) then this is clearly true, since by induction \(T\) is a subtree of \(M\) and \(e\in M\) and thus \(T\cup\{e\}\) is a subtree of \(M\). ◻

Second part of the proof is similar to Kruskal’s proof.

Time Complexity
How do we find the cheapest edge with exactly one endpoint in \(T\)?

Approach-1: Brute force: try all edges. \(O(E)\) time per edge finding. \(O(EV)\) time overall.
Approach-2: Maintain vertices in a Priority Queue (PQ) based on the weights of the least cost incident edge.

Delete min to determine the next edge \(e\) (incident to the corresponding vertex) to add to \(T\).
Discard \(e\) if both the endpoints are in \(T\).
Once \(e\) is added, update the weights of the least cost edges incident to the vertex added to \(T\).
\(O(\log{V})\) cost for extract min and decrease key. The overall cost is therefore \(O(V\log{V} + E\log{V}) = O(E\log{V})\).

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Boruvka’s Algorithm

Invented in 1926 by a Czech mathematician Otakar Boruvka (1899 - 1995). he is best known for his work in graph theory.
He designed this algorithm to solve a electrical network problem in Moravia.
This algorithm is more suitable for distributed and parallel computation.
This algorithm plays a pivotal role in a randomized linear time algorithm for MST due to Karger, Klein, and Tarjan (1995).

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Boruvka’s Algorithm

Start by creating a set \(S(v) = \{v\}\) for each vertex \(v\in V\) and an empty subgraph \(T=\phi\) initially.
In each round

For each set \(S\), find the minimum weight edge going out of \(S\), i.e, min\(\{w(u,v)| u\in S, v\notin S\}\). Let \(e_S\) be the edge computed for the set \(S\).
Add every edge \(e_S=(u,v)\) to the subgraph \(T\) and merge the sets of \(S(u)\) and \(S(v)\) into a single set \(S\).

Repeat the rounds until all vertices are merged into a single set and return \(T\).

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Correctness Proof

Any edge added by the algorithm in a round connects two different connected components.
What if the edges added in the same round form a cycle?This cannot happen because the weight of the picked edges in any path should be strictly decreasing. Thus, the edges cannot form a cycle. So, \(T\) is a tree.
By the cut rule, any edge inserted by the algorithm is the minimum weight edge going out of the connected component.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Time Complexity

Each round of the algorithm takes \(O(m)\) time as it involves going over all edges of the graph twice (one from each endpoint).
In each round, each connected component gets merged with at least one another, and thus the number of components decreases by, at least, a factor of two. So, after at most \(\log{n}\) rounds, only one component remains.
Thus, the overall time complexity is \(O(m\log{n})\).

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Exchange Argument

Greedy algorithm generally take the following form:

Select a candidate greedily according to some heuristic, and add it to your current solution if doing so doesn’t corrupt feasibility.
Repeat if not finished.

“Greedy Exchange" is one of the techniques used in proving the correctness of greedy algorithms.

The idea is to incrementally modify a solution produced by any other algorithm into the solution produced by your greedy algorithm in a way that doesn’t worsen the solution’s quality.
Thus the quality of your solution is at least as great as that of any other solution.
Thus, your algorithm does in fact return an optimal solution.

Matroid

Matroids are combinatorial structures in general. They generalizes the notion of linear independence in matrix theory.
A matroid \(M\) is defined on a finite ground set \(E\) and a collection of subsets of \(E\) said to be independent.
In general, a matroid \(M\) consists of a ground set and a family of independent sets \(M = (E,\mathcal{I})\) where

\(E\) is a finite set.
\((I_1)\):  if \(X\in\mathcal{I}\) and \(Y\subseteq X\) then \(Y\in\mathcal{I}\) (hereditary property),
\((I_2)\): if \(X\in\mathcal{I}\) and \(Y\in\mathcal{I}\) and \(|Y|>|X|\), then \(\exists e\in Y\setminus X\) such that \(X\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal{I}\) (exchange property).

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Example of a matroid
Consider a graphic matroid \(M_G = (S_G, \mathcal{I}_G)\) defined over an undirected graph \(G = (V,E)\) as follows:

The set \(S_G\) is defined to be \(E\), the set of edges of \(G\).
If \(A\) is a subset of \(E\), then \(A\in\mathcal{I}_G\) if and only if \(A\) is acyclic. That is, a set of edges \(A\) is independent if and only if the subgraph \(G_A = (V, A)\) forms a forest.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Example of Graphic Matroid

If \(G=(V, E)\) is an undirected graph, then \(M_G = (S_G, \mathcal{I}_G)\) is a matroid.


Proof. Proof. Idea: Clearly \(\mathcal{I}_G\) is hereditary since subset of a forest is a forest. We show that \(M_G\) satisfies the exchange property as follows:

Suppose \(G_A = (V, A)\) and \(G_B=(V, B)\) are forests of \(G\) such that \(|B|>|A|\).
We claim that a forest \(F = (V_F, E_F)\) contains exactly \(|V_F| - |E_F|\) trees.
Suppose \(F\) consists of \(t\) trees, where the \(i\)-th tree contains \(v_i\) vertices and \(e_i\) edges. From the property of the tree we know that \(e_i = v_i-1\). Then

 ◻

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Example of Graphic Matroid

Proof. 
Proof. $$
\[\begin{aligned}
        |E_F| &= \sum_{i=1}^te_i\\
            &= \sum_{i=1}^t (v_i-1)\\
            &=|V_F|-t
    
\end{aligned}\]
$$ Thus the forest \(G_A\) contains \(|V|-|A|\) trees and \(G_B\) contains \(|V|-|B|\) trees.
Since, \(G_B\) has fewer trees than forest \(G_A\), \(G_B\) must contain some tree \(T\) whose vertices are at least in two different trees in \(G_A\). Since \(T\) is connected, it must contain an edge \((u, v)\) such that vertices \(u\) and \(v\) are in different trees in forest \(G_A\). Since the edge \((u, v)\) connects vertices in two different trees in \(G_A\), we can add \((u, v)\) to forest \(G_A\) without creating a cycle. Thus, \(M_G\) satisfies the exchange property. ◻

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
More properties of matroid

Extension: Given a matroid \(M = (S, \mathcal{I})\), we call an element \(x\notin A\) an extension of \(A\in\mathcal{I}\) if \(A\cup\{x\}\in\mathcal{I}\).
Maximal: If \(A\) is an independent subset in \(M\), \(A\) is maximal if it has no extension.


All maximal independent subsets in a matroid have the same size.


Proof. Proof. Suppose to the contrary that \(A\) and \(B\) are two maximal independent subsets in a matroid \(M\) such that \(|B|>|A|\). Then, by the hereditary property, \(\exists x\in B-A\) such that \(A\cup\{x\}\) is also a maximal independent subset due to exchange property. This is a contradiction. ◻

Matrix Multiplication
The product \(C=A\times B\) of a \(p\times q\) matrix \(A\) and a \(q\times r\) matrix \(B\) is a \(p\times r\) matrix given by \[\begin{aligned}
    c[i,j] &= \displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^q a[i,k]b[k,j]

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Matrix Multiplication

While \(AB\) is defined, \(BA\) might not be defined.
It is possible that \(AB\neq BA\).
Multiplication is defined recursively: \(A_1A_2...A_{n-1}A_n = A_1(A_2\cdots (A_{n-1}A_n))\).
Matrix multiplication is associative, e.g, \(A_1A_2A_3 = (A_1A_2)A_3 = A_1(A_2A_3)\). Thus, parenthesization does not change the results.

Complexity of direct matrix multiplication \(C = A_{p\times q}\times B_{q\times r}\).

\(C\) has \(pr\) entries and each entry takes \(\Theta(q)\) times to compute. So the total cost is \(\Theta(pqr)\).

\((AB)C :\) The number of multiplication needed is \(pqr + prs\).
\(A(BC) :\) The number of multiplication needed is \(qrs + pqs\).

Setting \(p=5, q=4, r=6,\) and \(s=2\), we get

Problem Definition: Given \(n\) matrices \(A_1, A_2, ..., A_n\) with dimensions \(p_0, p_1, ..., p_n\) such that the dimensions of \(A_i\) be \(p_{i-1}\times p_i\), find the “multiplication sequence" that minimizes the number of scalar multiplication in computing \(A_1A_2...A_n\).
Exhaustive search: \(\Omega(4^n/n^{3/2})\) - approximation of Catalan number \(\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}\).
Any Better approach?
Yes. Dynamic programming.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Dynamic Programming Algorithm
Optimal Substructure: Determine the structure of an optimal solution (a parenthesization in this case).
For each pair \(1\leq i\leq j\leq n\), determine the multiplication sequence for \(A_{i...j} = A_iA_{i+1}...A_j\) that minimizes the number of scalar multiplication.
Clearly, \(A_{i...j}\) is a \(p_{i-1}\times p_j\) matrix.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Dynamic Programming Algorithm
Parenthesization for \(A_{i...j}\): For any optimal multiplication sequence, at the last step, we are multiplying two matrices \(A_{i...k}\) and \(A_{k+1...j}\) for some \(k\). That is, \[\begin{aligned}
    A_{i...j} &= (A_i...A_k)(A_{k+1}...A_j) = A_{i...k}A_{k+1...j}.
\end{aligned}\] Example: \(A_{3...6} = (A_3(A_4A_5))(A_6) = A_{3...5}A_{6...6}\).
Here, \(k=5\).

How do we decide \(k\)? .
How do we parenthesize \(A_{i...k}\)? .

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Dynamic Programming Algorithm
If the optimal solution of \(A_{i...j}\) involves splitting into \(A_{i...k}\) and \(A_{k+1...j}\) at the final step then parenthesization of \(A_{i...k}\) and \(A_{k+1...j}\) in the final optimal solution must also be optimal for the subproblems. Why?

If parenthesization of \(A_{i...k}\) was not optimal we could replace it by a better parenthesization and get a cheaper final solution, leading to a contradiction.
Similarly, if parenthesization of \(A_{k+1...j}\) was not optimal we could replace it by a better parenthesization and get a cheaper final solution, leading to a contradiction.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Dynamic Programming Algorithm
Define the value of an optimal solution to a subproblem: For \(1\leq i\leq j\leq n\), let \(m[i,j]\) denote the minimum number of multiplication required to compute \(A_{i...j}\). Then the optimal cost can be defined as follows: \[m[i,j] = \begin{cases}
        0 & i=j,\\
        \mbox{min}_{i\leq k<j}(m[i,k] + m[k+1,j] + p_{i-1}p_kp_j) & i<j
\end{cases}\]

Proof. Proof. Any optimal sequence of multiplication for \(A_{i...j}\) is equivalent to some choice of splitting \(A_{i...j} = A_{i...k}A_{k+1...j}\) for some \(k\), where the sequence of multiplications for \(A_{i...k}\) and \(A_{k+1...j}\) are also optimal. Hence the formulation follows. ◻

This course is an advanced study that follows Data Structures and Algorithms. Identify and apply suitable algorithmic paradigms and data structures to solve a given problem.

Rigorously argue and establish the time complexity of algorithms.

Develop formal proofs for the correctness of algorithms.

Understand the fundamental role of data structures in efficient algorithm implementation.

Encoding and Decoding Problem

Fixed length code: Each codeword has the same length.
Variable length code: Codewords may have different length.
Example:




image



Fixed length code requires \(300,000\) bits to store the file.
Number of bits required to store the file using variable length code is: \((45\cdot 1 + 13\cdot 3 + 12\cdot 3 + 16\cdot 3 + 9\cdot 4 + 5\cdot 4)\cdot 1000 = 224,000\) bits.
Saving using variable length code is around \(25\%\).
In what follows a code is a set of codewords, e.g, \(\{000, 001, 010, 011, 100, 101\}\) and \(\{0, 101, 100, 111, 1101, 1100\}\).

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Encoding
Given a code corresponding to some alphabet \(\Gamma\) and a message, it is easy to encode the message by replacing the characters with codewords. For example, let \(\Gamma = \{a,b,c,d\}\).

Suppose the code is \(C_1: \{a=00, b=01, c=10, d=11\}\). Encoding of “bad" using \(C_1\) is 010011.
Suppose the code is \(C_2: \{a=0, b=110, c=10, d=111\}\). Encoding of “bad" using \(C_2\) is 1101111.
Suppose the code is \(C_3: \{a=1, b=110, c=10, d=111\}\). Encoding of “bad" using \(C_3\) is 1101111.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Decoding
Given an encoded message, decoding is the process of retrieving the original message. A message is uniquely decodable if it can only be decoded in one way.

Relative to \(C_1\), 010011 is uniquely decodable to “bad".
Relative to \(C_2\), 1101111 is uniquely decodable to “bad".
Relative to \(C_3\), 1101111 is not uniquely decodable. It can be decoded to either “bad" or”acad".

Prefix-Codes

Fixed length codes are always uniquely decodable (Why?).
Fixed length codes do not provide best compression!
Prefix Code: A code is called prefix code if no codeword is a prefix of one another.
Every message encoded by a prefix code is uniquely decodable. Since no codeword is a prefix of the other, we can always find the first codeword, peel it off, and continue decoding.
Goal: Find a good prefix code.

The Problem: Given an alphabet \(A=\{a_1, a_2, ..., a_n\}\) with frequency distribution \(f(a_i)\), find a binary prefix code \(C\) for \(A\) that minimizes the number of bits: \(B(C) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}f(a_i)L(c(a_i))\) needed to encode a message of \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(a_i)\) characters, where \(c(a_i)\) is the codeword for encoding \(a_i\) and \(L(c(a_i))\) is the length of the codeword \(c(a_i)\).

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms

Huffman Coding
Step-1: Pick two letters \(x\) and \(y\) from alphabet \(A\) with the smallest frequencies and create a subtree that has these two characters as leaves. ( Greedy idea). Label the root of this subtree as \(z\).
Step-2: Set frequency \(f(z) = f(x)+f(y)\). Remove \(x, y\) and add \(z\) creating new alphabet \(A' = A\cup\{z\}-\{x,y\}\).
Repeat this procedure, called merge, with new alphabet \(A'\) until an alphabet with only one symbol is left.
The resulting tree is the Huffman code.

Some other edge in \(C\), say \(e\), has exactly one endpoint in \(S\).

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms

Sort the edges by their weights.
Initialize \(F=\phi\).
Consider the edges from lowest to highest weights. For each edge \(e\), add it to \(F\) if it does not create any cycle in \(F\).

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Correctness of Kruskal’s Algorithm

Kruskal’s algorithm correctly computes an MST


Proof. Proof. We will prove by induction that \(F\) is always a subgraph of some MST. This is obviously true at the beginning, since \(F\) is empty. Suppose it is true at some point in our algorithm: \(F\) is currently a subgraph of some MST \(M\), and Kruskal’s algorithm adds an edge \(e\). We want to show that there is some MST \(M'\) such that \(F\cup\{e\}\) is a subgraph of \(M'\). ◻

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Correctness of Kruskal’s Algorithm

Proof. Continues.… If \(e\in M\) then this is trivially true: we set \(M = M'\), and since \(F\subseteq M\) and \(e\in M\), we know that \(F\cup\{e\}\subseteq M\). Otherwise, consider we add \(e\) to \(M\). Since Kruskal’s algorithm added \(e\), this means that adding \(e\) did not create any cycle, so the two endpoints of \(e\) must be in different trees in \(F\). So, if we follow the cycle in \(M\), there must be some other edge \(e'\) whose two endpoints also lie in different trees in \(F\). This means that Kruskal’s algorithm could have added \(e'\), but instead choose to add \(e\). Thus \(w(e)\leq w(e')\). So, if we remove \(e'\) from \(M\) and add \(e\) to get a new tree \(M'\), we know that the weight of \(M'\) is at most the weight of \(M\) is thus an MST, and \(F\cup\{e\}\) is a subgraph of \(M'\). Thus the theorem follows. ◻

Total number of operations is \(n\).
The \(n\) operations can be a mix of PUSH, POP, MULTI-POP

A simple time complexity analysis:

The worst case time for MULTI-POP in the sequence is \(O(n)\), since the stack size is at most \(n\).

This is correct, but a loose bound.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Amortized analysis: aggregate method

Consider a sequence of \(n\) PUSH, POP, MULTI-POP operations on an initially empty stack.
MULTI-POPs are nothing but a sequence of POPs, so analysis can consider only number of PUSH and POPs (either direct POP or POPs within a MULTI-POP).
Each element pushed can be popped at most once.
So the no. of POP operations (including POPs within a MULTI-POP) \(\leq\) number of PUSH operations.
Thus the total time is at most \(O(n)\) since PUSH and POP are \(O(1)\) each.
Hence the average cost of operation is \(O(n)/n = O(1)\).
We say that the amortized cost of a PUSH, POP, or MULTI-POP in a sequence of \(n\) operations in \(O(1)\).

Dynamic Table
Goal: Store items in a table (Example: hash table, binary heap etc.)

Two operations: INSERT and DELETE.

too many items inserted \(\implies\) expand table.
too many items deleted \(\implies\) contract table.

Requirement: If the table contains \(m\) items, then space = \(\Theta(m)\).

Suppose we are performing a sequence of \(n\) insert operations:

If there is a space in the table to insert, then the insertion cost is \(O(1)\).
If there is no space to insert, we need to expand the table, and then insert the element into the new table. This costs \(O(n)\) because,

We need to first copy all the elements from old table to new table.
Insert the element in the new table


Thus, an intermixed sequence of \(n\) INSERT and DELETE takes \(O(n^2)\) time.

Max Flow Min Cut Theorem

If \(f\) is a flow in a flow network \(G = (V, E)\) with source \(s\) and sink \(t\), then the following conditions are equivalent:

(1) \(f\) is a maximum flow in \(G\).
(2) The residual network \(G_f\) contains no augmenting paths.
(3) \(|f| = cap(S, T)\) for some cut \((S, T)\) of \(S\) such that \(s\in S\) and \(t\in T\).

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
section: Proof: Max Flow Min Cut Theorem
text:
Proof: Max Flow Min Cut Theorem

Proof. Proof.

\((1)\implies (2):\) Suppose for the sake of contradiction that \(f\) is a maximum flow in \(G\) but that \(G_f\) has an augmenting path \(p\). Then the flow generated by augmenting \(f\) by the minimum capacity of the augmenting path in \(G_f\) is a flow in \(G\) strictly greater than \(|f|\), contradicting the assumption that \(f\) is a maximum flow.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
section: Proof: Max Flow Min Cut Theorem
text:
Proof: Max Flow Min Cut Theorem

Proof. Proof.

\((2)\implies (3):\) Suppose that \(G_f\) has no augmenting path, that is, that \(G_f\) contains not path from \(s\) to \(t\). Define $S={vV : }$ and \(T = V\setminus S\). THe partition \((S, T)\) is a cut: we have \(s\in S\) and \(t\notin S\) because there is not path from \(s\) to \(t\) in \(G_f\). Now consider a pair of vertices \(u\in S\) and \(v\in T\). If \((u,v)\in E\), we must have \(f(u,v) = c(u,v)\), since otherwise, \((u,v)\in E_f\), which would place \(v\) in \(S\). If \((v,u)\in E\), we must have \(f(v,u)=0\), because otherwise \(c_f(u,v) = f(v,u)\) would be positive and we would have \((u,v)\in E_f\), which would place \(v\) in \(S\). Of course, if neither \((u,v)\) nor \((v,u)\) is in \(E\), then \(f(u,v) = f(v,u) = 0\). Thus $$
\[\begin{aligned}
    f(S,T)  &= \sum_{u\in S}\sum_{v\in T}f(u,v) - \sum_{v\in T}\sum_{u\in S}f(v,u) \\
            &= \sum_{u\in S}\sum_{v\in T}c(u,v) \\
            &= c(S,T).

\end{aligned}\]
$$

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Introduction
Given a problem X and a machine model M, how long does it take to solve X using a machine from M?
Instead of answering this difficult question directly, we ask:

How can we classify problems into complexity classes based on their apparent difficulty?
What relationships can we establish between these complexity classes?

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
P vs. NP
The most famous of these questions center around the P vs. NP problem.

P: Problems that can be solved in time polynomial in the size of the input on a reasonable computational device.
NP: Problems whose solutions can be verified in time polynomial in the size of the input.

The big question: Are there any problems in NP that are not also in P?

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Other Complexity Classes
Computational complexity theory also includes questions about other computational resources.

L (Log Space): Problems solvable using space logarithmic in the size of the input. Any problem solvable in L is also solvable in P.
NL: Non-deterministic log space. Open question: Is L = NL?
PSPACE: Problems solvable using polynomial space.
BPP: Bounded-error probabilistic polynomial-time computations. Open question: Is BPP = P?

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Problems and Languages
Most problems studied in complexity theory are decision problems.

Given an input \(x\), answer “yes” or “no” based on whether \(x\) satisfies some predicate \(P\).
Example: GRAPH 3-COLORABILITY: Given a graph \(G\), is there a way to assign three colors to the vertices so that no edge has two endpoints of the same color?

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Why Decision Problems?

Decision problems are simpler to reason about than more general functions.
Decision problems capture most of what is hard about function computation.

Inputs are encoded over some alphabet \(\Sigma\) (typically \(\{0,1\}\)).
Formally, a language \(L\) is a set of finite strings over \(\Sigma\). If \(x \in L\), the output should be “yes”; otherwise “no”.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Models of Computation

Logic Circuit: Consists of logic gates realizing Boolean functions. Basic building blocks of all digital computers.
Finite-State Machine (FSM): A machine with memory. Executes steps taking current state and external input to produce output.
Random-Access Machine (RAM): A pair of interconnected FSMs — a CPU and a random-access memory. Holds data and programs (instructions for the CPU).
Other models: Push-down automata, Turing machines.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Decision vs. Optimization Problems
For a problem \(X\):

Search Problem: Find a solution that satisfies \(X\).
Optimization Problem: Find a solution that satisfies \(X\) and minimizes (maximizes) an objective function.
Decision Problem: Determine if there is any solution for \(X\).

Example: SHORTEST PATH (Optimization) vs. PATH (Decision): - SHORTEST PATH: Find a path from \(u\) to \(v\) using the fewest edges. - PATH: Does a path exist from \(u\) to \(v\) consisting of at most \(k\) edges?

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
The Class P and NP

P: All decision problems for which solutions can be efficiently (polynomial time) found.
NP (Non-deterministic Polynomial): All decision problems that can be “verified” in polynomial time.

A problem \(D\) can be verified in polynomial time if there is a verifier \(V\) taking two inputs \(x\) (instance) and \(c\) (certificate) such that: - For all yes-instances \(x\), there exists \(c\) such that \(V(x, c)\) outputs yes. - For all no-instances \(x\), for all \(c\), \(V(x, c)\) outputs no.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Examples
COMPOSITE: Given positive integer \(x\), does \(x\) have any factors? - Verifier \(V(x, c)\): Check \(1 < c < x\) and \(c\) divides \(x\).
VERTEX COVER: Given graph \(G\) and integer \(k\), does \(G\) contain a vertex cover of size \(k\)? - Verifier \(V(\{G,k\}, c)\): Verify \(c\) is a subset of exactly \(k\) vertices and forms a vertex cover.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Reductions
A technique to formalize that one problem is not “harder” than another.
\(D_1 \le_p D_2\) if there is a function \(f\) computable in polynomial time such that for all inputs \(x\): \[x \in D_1 \iff f(x) \in D_2\]
If \(D_1 \le_p D_2\) and \(D_2\) is in P, then \(D_1\) is in P.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
NP-Completeness
Decision problem \(D\) is NP-Complete if:

\(D\) is in NP
\(D\) is NP-hard: for all \(D'\) in NP, \(D' \le_p D\)

Theorem: If \(D\) is NP-complete, then \(D \in P\) iff \(P = NP\).
Cook’s Theorem: SAT is NP-Complete.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Summary

Complexity classes classify problems by resource requirements
P: efficiently solvable, NP: efficiently verifiable
Decision problems capture the essence of hard problems
Models of computation: RAM, FSM, Logic Circuits, Turing Machines
NP-Completeness: hardest problems in NP via polynomial reductions

CLIQUE NP-hardness: Proof (\(\Rightarrow\))
Suppose formula \(F\) is satisfiable.

In the satisfying assignment, at least one literal is true in every clause.
In each triple of \(G\), select one node corresponding to a true literal.
These \(k\) nodes form a \(k\)-clique:

Only one node per triple (no same-triple conflict)
No complementary labels (both literals are true)

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
CLIQUE NP-hardness: Proof (\(\Leftarrow\))
Suppose \(G\) has a \(k\)-clique.

No two of the clique’s nodes occur in the same triple.
Each of the \(k\) triples contains exactly one \(k\)-clique node.
Assign truth values so each literal labeling a clique node is made true.
Since each triple contains a clique node, each clause contains a true literal, so \(F\) is satisfiable.

Vertex Cover
A vertex cover of a graph \(G = (V, E)\) is a subset \(S \subseteq V\) such that every edge \((u, v)\) is incident to at least one vertex in \(S\).
The VERTEX COVER (VC) decision problem: Does \(G\) have a vertex cover of size \(k\)?

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
VC is in NP
Given \(G = (V, E)\) and a set \(S\) (certificate):

For each vertex \(v \in S\), remove all incident edges.
Check if all edges are removed from \(G\).

Thus, VC is in NP.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
VC is NP-hard
Reduction from IND-SET to VC:
Given an IND-SET instance \(G = (V, E)\) and integer \(k\):

Construct \(G' = G\) (identical copy) with \(k' = |V| - k\).
This takes \(O(|V| + |E|)\) time.

Claim: \(G\) has an independent set of size \(k\) iff \(G'\) has a vertex cover of size \(k'\).

(\(\Leftarrow\)) Suppose \(S\) is a vertex cover of size \(k\). Then \(V \setminus S\) is an independent set of size \(|V| - k\).

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Vertex Cover: Analysis of 2-Approximation
APPROX-VERTEX-COVER (review): - Pick any edge \((u,v)\), add both \(u\) and \(v\) to cover. - Remove all incident edges. - Repeat until no edges remain.
Why 2-approximation? The set of edges picked form a matching (no two share a vertex). Any vertex cover must contain at least one endpoint of each picked edge, so \(|\text{OPT}| \ge |\text{matching}|\).

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Vertex Cover: Example
Consider a star graph with center \(c\) and leaves \(l_1, \dots, l_n\).

Optimal cover: \(\{c\}\) with size 1.
Greedy (max degree) picks \(c\) first — optimal!

But consider a graph where greedy picks poorly:

A graph with edges forming a perfect matching.
Greedy picks both endpoints of each edge in sequence.
Optimal picks one endpoint per edge.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Greedy Set Cover: Analysis
Let \(c\) be the size of the optimum set cover and \(g\) be the size of the greedy set cover.
Let \(m_0 = m\) be the initial number of uncovered elements. Let \(m_i\) be the number remaining after \(i\) iterations.
After \(i-1\) rounds, \(m_{i-1}\) elements remain. Since there is a cover of size \(c\), by the pigeonhole principle, some set covers at least \(m_{i-1}/c\) elements.
So the greedy algorithm (which picks the largest set) covers at least \(m_{i-1}/c\) elements, giving: \[m_i \le m_{i-1} - \frac{m_{i-1}}{c} = m_{i-1}\left(1 - \frac{1}{c}\right)\]

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Greedy Set Cover: Bound
After \(i\) iterations: \[m_i \le m\left(1 - \frac{1}{c}\right)^i \le m \cdot e^{-i/c}\]
Since the greedy cover size is \(g\), after \(g\) iterations we have \(m_g < 1\) (all elements covered): \[m \cdot e^{-g/c} < 1\]
Solving: \[g > c \ln m\]
Thus \(|G| \le |O| \ln m\) where \(m\) is the total number of elements.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Summary

Vertex Cover: 2-approximation via edge-picking matching
Set Cover: \(\ln m\)-approximation via greedy (pigeonhole principle)
Both use simple, intuitive strategies with provable guarantees
Approximation algorithms are practical tools for NP-hard problems

Decision Tree Argument




image




A decision tree is a mathematical representation of a sorting algorithm for a fixed value of \(n\).
Each node of the decision tree represents a comparison made in the algorithm(e.g. \(a1:a2\)).
The two branches represent the possible results. For example, the left subtree consists of the remaining comparisons made under the assumption that \(a_1\leq a_2\) and the right subtree for \(a_1>a_2\).
the leaves of the decision tree are the permutations of the \(n\) numbers each through a unique path.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Analysis

Consider any sorting algorithm.
Let \(T(n)\) be the maximum number of comparisons that the algorithm makes on any input of size \(n\).
The running time of the algorithm must be at least as large as \(T(n)\) - we are not counting data movement or other computations.
The algorithm defines a decision tree.
Observe that the height of the decision tree is \(T(n)\) - the path from the root to a leaf corresponds to a sequence of comparisons made by the algorithm.

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Analysis

Observation 1. Any binary tree of height \(T(n)\) has at most \(2^{T(n)}\) leaves.

This means - the sorting algorithm can distinguish among at most \(2^{T(n)}\) different final actions.

The number of possible permutations with \(n\) numbers is \(n!\).
Therefore the number of leaves \(2^{T(n)}\) in the decision tree should be at least \(n!\).

title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms
text:
Analysis
Therefore,
\[\begin{aligned}
    2^{T(n)} & \geq n!\\
    \implies T(n) &\geq \log_2{(n!)}\\
        & \geq \log_2({\sqrt{2\pi n}(\frac{n}{e})^n}) \mbox{ using Sitrling's approximation }\\
        & = \log_2{\sqrt{2\pi n}} + n\log_2{n} - n\log_2{e} \in \Omega(n\log_2{n})
\end{aligned}\]

The natural proofs barrier against data-structure lower-bounds [STOC’26]


Bruno Loff, Michal Koucký, Tulasimohan Molli, Michael Saks


  Abstract 
  Slides 
  Cite 
  Manuscript 



@inproceedings{LKMS26, author = {Loff, Bruno and Koucký, Michal and Molli, Tulasimohan and Saks, Michael}, title = {The natural proofs barrier against data-structure lower-bounds}, booktitle = {58th Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing (STOC)}, year = {2026} }


Consider a data structure problem with possible data coming from a set \mathcal D, queries coming from a set \mathcal Q, and in the dynamic case updates coming from a set \mathcal U. Then, the current state of the art in data structure lower bounds is t = \tilde\Omega(\log |\mathcal Q|) for static data structure problems, and \max(t_{\mathrm q},t_{\mathrm u}) = \tilde\Omega((\log n)^2) where n = \max(|\mathcal Q|,|\mathcal U|,\log |\mathcal D|) for dynamic.
We port Razborov and Rudich’s natural-proofs framework to the setting of static and dynamic data structures in the cell probe model, in a way that strongly suggests this state of the art is unlikely to be improved anytime soon. A similar direction was recently taken also by Korten, Pitassi and Impagliazzo (FOCS 2025) who look at static data structure lower bounds in a different regime of parameters. Our contribution is:

We define notions analogous to pseudorandom functions (PRF). We call these primitives local PRFs, in the context of static data structures, and local and locally updatable (LLU) PRFs, in the context of dynamic data structures.
We then formulate cryptographic conjectures, namely, that secure local PRFs and secure LLU PRFs exist, precisely at the frontier where we are no longer able to prove static, respectively dynamic, data structure lower bounds. If these conjectures are true, it follows that the current state of the art in data structure lower bounds cannot be improved by a natural proof.
We show that (almost) every single known data structure lower bound proof is a natural proof, by surveying all lower bounds in the literature (known to us). (The only exception is proofs based on lifting theorems.)
It follows that, if our cryptographic conjecture is true, then all known lower bound proof techniques (minus the one exception) are unable to improve upon the state of the art. (We also attempt to address the exception.)
Further, we provide concrete candidate constructions for our two pseudo-ran-dom primitives. We conjecture that our constructions are secure for parameters just above the state-of-the-art lower bounds.
We also show that, whether or not they are secure, our candidate PRFs at least satisfy the natural properties appearing in all (but one) known proofs.
So if one is interested in improving upon the state of the art in static or dynamic data structure lower bounds, one must find a non-natural method of proving such lower bounds (no such method currently exists), or one may as well begin by trying to break our PRF candidates.

A p-random restriction is a random partial input obtained by independently setting each variable to either 0,1 with (1-p)/2 each or leaving it unset with probability p. In this work, we study decision trees of bounded depth formulas under p-random restrictions.
Criticality of a boolean function f is defined to be the probability p at which the decision tree depth t of a random restriction of f goes down exponentially in t. Criticality has been implicitly studied in circuit complexity in the works of {all criticality results here}. The ground breaking work of Hastad’s switching lemma is a bound on criticality of CNFs and DNFs. Rossman defined the notion of criticality and showed its connection to average case lower bounds, fourier tail bounds, learning algorithms and decision tree size.
In this we work we show optimal bound on criticality of \AC^0 which for a formula of depth d+1 and size S is \bra{\frac{\log S}{d}}^d. Prior to this work, Rossman showed a similar bound for regular formulas: the class of \AC^0 formulas in which all gates at any given depth have the same fan-in. We extend their proof the general \AC^0 formulas.

Chang’s lemma (Duke Mathematical Journal, 2002) is a classical result in mathematics, with applications spanning across additive combinatorics, combinatorial number theory, analysis of Boolean functions, communication complexity and algorithm design. For a Boolean function f that takes values in \pmone let r(f) denote its Fourier rank (i.e., the dimension of the span of its Fourier support). For each positive threshold t, Chang’s lemma provides a lower bound on \delta(f):=\Pr[f(x)=-1] in terms of the dimension of the span of its characters with Fourier coefficients of magnitude at least 1/t. In this work we examine the tightness of Chang’s lemma with respect to the following three natural settings of the threshold:

the Fourier sparsity of f, denoted k(f),
the Fourier max-supp-entropy of f, denoted k'(f), defined to be the maximum value of the reciprocal of the absolute value of a non-zero Fourier coefficient,
the Fourier max-rank-entropy of f, denoted k''(f), defined to be the minimum t such that characters whose coefficients are at least 1/t in magnitude span a r(f)-dimensional space. In this work we prove new lower bounds on \delta(f) in terms of the above measures. One of our lower bounds, \delta(f)=\Omega\left(r(f)^2/(k(f) \log^2 k(f))\right), subsumes and refines the previously best known upper bound on r(f) in terms of k(f) by Sanyal (Theory of Computing, 2019). Another lower bound, \delta(f) =\Omega\left(r(f)/(\seerank(f) \log k(f))\right), is based on our improvement of a bound by Chattopadhyay, Hatami, Lovett and Tal (ITCS, 2019) on the sum of absolute values of level-1 Fourier coefficients in terms of \ftwo-degree. We further show that Chang’s lemma for the above-mentioned choices of the threshold is asymptotically outperformed by our bounds for most settings of the parameters involved.

Next, we show that our bounds are tight for a wide range of the parameters involved, by constructing functions witnessing their tightness. All the functions we construct are modifications of the Addressing function, where we replace certain input variables by suitable functions. Our final contribution is to construct Boolean functions f for which

our lower bounds asymptotically match \delta(f), and
for any choice of the threshold t, the lower bound obtained from Chang’s lemma is asymptotically smaller than \delta(f). Our results imply more refined deterministic one-way communication complexity upper bounds for XOR functions. Given the wide-ranging application of Chang’s lemma, we strongly feel that our refinements of Chang’s lemma will find many more applications.

For \eps \in (0,1/3), the \eps-error probabilistic degree of any Boolean function f:\zo^n\to \zo over \reals is the smallest non-negative integer d such that the following holds: there exists a distribution \distP of polynomials P(x_1,\ldots,x_n)  \in \reals[x_1,\ldots,x_n] of degree at most d such that for all \bar{x} \in \zo^n, we have \Pr_{P \sim \distP}[P(\bar{x}) = f(\bar{x}) ] \geq 1- \eps. Sci. 1993) and Beigel, Reingold, and Spielman (Proc. 6th CCC 1991), that the \eps-error probabilistic degree of the \OR function is at most O(\log n \cdot \lepsinv). Our first observation is that this can be improved to \bigo{\ans} which is better for small values of \eps.
In all known constructions of probabilistic polynomials for the \OR function (including the above improvement), the polynomials P in the support of the distribution \distP have the following special structure:
[ P(x_1,,x_n) = 1 - _{i } (1- L_i(x_1,,x_n)), ]
where each L_i(x_1,\dots, x_n) is a linear form in the variables x_1,\ldots,x_n, i.e., the polynomial 1-P(\bar{x}) is a product of affine forms.
